[Elementary Statistics](../index.qmd) / Confidence intervals

## What are we trying to understand?

~~~{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../../assets/interactive/interactive-lessons.css">
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../../assets/interactive/confidence-interval-lesson.css">
<div class="clt-lesson ci-lesson">
<p>Imagine estimating the average score on a hypothetical attention test. In Week 6, you saw that repeated samples from the same population produce different sample means. If we only get to collect one sample, how can we communicate how uncertain that estimate is?</p>
<p>A <strong>confidence interval</strong> combines a sample estimate with a margin of error. In this optional Week 7 lesson, you will repeat the process and see which intervals contain the true population mean.</p>
<div class="clt-overview"><p><strong>Learning goals</strong></p><ol><li>Interpret a confidence level as the long-run coverage of an interval procedure.</li><li>Explain how increasing sample size affects interval width.</li><li>Explain the trade-off between confidence level and precision.</li><li>Distinguish observed coverage from the theoretical confidence level.</li></ol><p><strong>Before starting:</strong> Review normal probability, sampling distributions, and standard error from Weeks 5–6.</p></div>
</div>
~~~

## Make a prediction

<h3>How is the interval constructed?</h3><table class="clt-summary"><caption>Current settings and most recent sample</caption><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Sample size (n)</th><td data-output="n">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Confidence level</th><td data-output="confidence">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Standard error (10 / √n)</th><td data-output="se">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Critical z-value</th><td data-output="critical">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Margin of error</th><td data-output="margin">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Interval width</th><td data-output="width">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Most recent sample mean</th><td data-output="mean">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Most recent confidence interval</th><td data-output="interval">—</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Does it contain 50?</th><td data-output="latest-result">—</td></tr></tbody></table><p class="clt-caption">The model uses known population SD, so intervals have identical widths for a fixed sample size and confidence level. When the population SD is unknown, we usually estimate it and use a t-based interval under appropriate conditions.</p></section>

## Interpret what you find

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson ci-lesson">
<ol><li>Set n = 10 and confidence = 95%. Draw one sample at a time. Does every interval include the true mean? Draw 20 and then 1,000 more. How does observed coverage compare with 95%?</li><li>At 95% confidence, compare n = 10 and n = 40. Record the standard error and interval width before changing settings. What happens to precision? Does the target coverage change?</li><li>At n = 10, compare 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence. Draw 1,000 intervals for each. Which has the greatest width? Which should have the highest long-run coverage?</li></ol><p><strong>Think about it:</strong> If two students use the same settings, must they obtain exactly the same coverage percentage? Why or why not?</p>
</div>
~~~

## What is a confidence interval telling us?

~~~{=html}
<div class="clt-lesson ci-lesson">
<p>A point estimate is a single number, such as a sample mean. An interval estimate gives a range of plausible parameter values, reflecting sampling uncertainty under the model.</p><div class="ci-formula"><strong>Confidence interval for a population mean (known SD)</strong><br>Sample mean ± critical z-value × standard error<br>Standard error = σ / √n<br>Margin of error = critical z-value × standard error</div><p>For example, if n = 25, the standard error is 10 / √25 = 2. At 95% confidence, the margin of error is approximately 1.96 × 2 = 3.92. If our sample mean is 52, the interval is [48.08, 55.92]. It contains the true mean of 50.</p><p><strong>Why this makes sense:</strong> Larger samples produce less variable means, so we can use narrower intervals. Higher confidence means we want the procedure to succeed more often, which requires wider intervals for the same sample size. The actual population mean does not move when we draw a new sample; the interval moves.</p><p>In repeated sampling under the model, 95% confidence means that about 95% of intervals constructed by this procedure will contain the fixed population mean. It does not mean 95% of the observations lie inside the interval, or that a particular computed interval has a 95% frequentist probability of containing the fixed parameter. In real research, the true mean is unknown; we show it here only so that you can observe coverage.</p><p>The exact coverage in this simulation relies on independent normal observations and a known population standard deviation. We will address estimated variability and t intervals separately.</p>
</div>
~~~

If we construct 20 intervals at 95% confidence, what should we expect?</legend><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ci-variation" value="exact"> Exactly 19 must contain the true mean.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ci-variation" value="vary"> The number that contain the true mean can vary across runs.</label><label class="clt-choice"><input type="radio" name="ci-variation" value="all"> All 20 must contain the true mean.</label><button type="button" class="clt-btn clt-secondary">Check answer</button><p class="clt-feedback" data-output="feedback" role="status" aria-live="polite"></p></fieldset><p><strong>Takeaway:</strong> Confidence describes the procedure; precision describes the width. Sample size and confidence level affect width in different ways.</p><p>Textbook connection: <a href="https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/8-1-a-single-population-mean-using-the-normal-distribution">OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, Section 8.1 — A Single Population Mean Using the Normal Distribution</a>.</p>
